title: Environment is not the most important variable in determining oral morphine consumption in Wistar rats

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether a richer, shared living space makes animals take less of a drug, and these animal studies cannot show anything about people. In three small experiments from one laboratory (Simon Fraser University; 1978, 1979 and 1981; the original papers are not read here and are described by a critical history), rats housed together in a large enclosure with sawdust, boxes and tubes ('Rat Park') drank less morphine solution than rats housed alone in small cages, but only under particular conditions: on choice days after a period of forced morphine drinking (1978), with sweetened, weak solutions (1979), and according to the housing at the time of testing, not in early life (1981). During 57 days when morphine solution was their only fluid, the Rat Park rats drank more on average (18.6 against 13.3 mg of morphine hydrochloride per rat, as tabulated), and they did drink morphine, contrary to popular accounts. The groups held 8 to 22 rats, males and females lived together in Rat Park with no account of pregnancies, intake was measured by different methods in the two housing conditions, and the many comparisons raised the risk of chance findings; the original authors drew cautious conclusions and did not link the results to drug problems in people (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). Two experiments designed to repeat the 1981 study, each with 10 male and 10 female rats in each housing condition, did not find lower intake in colony rats: in the first, colony rats drank slightly more of the strongest solution (3.6 against 0.0 g a day) and no differently at the three weaker ones; in the second, with the colony's intake known only as a group total and no statistical test, isolated rats drank more at three of four strengths, by smaller margins than the up to sevenfold difference described for 1981 (Petrie, 1996). The author's explanation, a change in the supplier's breeding stock, was not tested, and this study too measured intake differently in the two housing conditions. Other housing studies, summarized second-hand, point both ways: in one, rats reared in enriched or impoverished conditions did not differ in morphine intake and the enriched rats drank more cocaine solution; in another, isolated rats quickly learned to give themselves intravenous cocaine while socially housed rats did not consistently (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In a different kind of experiment, male rats offered a choice between an intravenous cocaine infusion and a sweet drink almost all came to prefer the sweet drink, also after a period of escalating cocaine intake and while under the influence of cocaine, though they still chose cocaine on about 16% of choices (Lenoir et al., 2007); earlier studies in monkeys, as those authors note, found most monkeys preferring high doses of cocaine to food. Every finding here comes from animals under laboratory conditions; how housing, poverty, opportunity or social exclusion shape drug use and drug problems in people is not shown by these designs. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of environment. Rat Park, as tabulated by Gage & Sumnall (2019): 1978, forced access (57 days) Rat Park 18.6 vs isolated 13.3 mg morphine hydrochloride per rat; Nichols cycles F = 200.9 (df 1/69) and abstinence period F 26.38 (df 1/23), isolated rats drinking more on choice days; 1979, housing difference only with 10% sucrose, largest at 0.15 mg/ml; 1981, housing at testing F = 33.64, p < 0.0001 (df not printed). Petrie (1996), isolated vs colony, grams of morphine solution a day: Experiment 1, 1.0 mg/ml 0.0 vs 3.6 (colony more; F(1, 34) = 80.98 for grams), 0.5 mg/ml 0.5 vs 1.3, 0.25 mg/ml 15.7 vs 18.3, 0.125 mg/ml 30.2 vs 42.8 (no housing difference at these three); Experiment 2 (no test), 0.3 vs 4.3, 9.4 vs 3.0, 17.4 vs 10.9, 44.4 vs 33.1; the 1981 difference described as up to sevenfold. Lenoir et al. (2007), male rats, intravenous cocaine (0.25 mg per infusion, study condition) vs 20 s of 0.2% saccharin: saccharin preferred from day 2 (N = 43); rats preferring cocaine 2.3% (drug-naive), 8.3% (first trained on cocaine), none of 11 (after intake escalated from 7.34 to 26.04 mg/day); cocaine chosen on about 15.6% of choices on average.
